passages.frankenstein-1831-chapter-4-life-and-dea: Victor Frankenstein remembers the ambition that carried him toward his experiment, speaking in images of hurricanes, torrents, light, darkness, life and death. The passage moves between exhilaration and consequence before the creature itself appears. Its language makes creation feel both intimate and immense: a maker imagines gratitude, kinship and renewal while corruption waits at the edge of the page. Read slowly for the words that turn aspiration into warning, or darkness into a different kind of illumination. You do not need to follow Victor’s meaning. Keep only the path that answers you, while Mary Shelley’s source and its uneasy questions remain visible around it.
passages.persuasion-1818-chapter-4-prudence-and-r: Anne Elliot looks back at the advice that separated her from an early attachment. Jane Austen compresses years of feeling into a few poised oppositions: youth and age, caution and confidence, prudence and romance. The sentence does not offer an easy verdict. It lets good sense feel protective and wounding at once, while the future remains something a person can trust or fear. This compact page rewards attention to its turns and repetitions. You might notice a poem about risk, regret, time, or becoming, but the choice remains yours. Keep the words that speak now and let Austen’s balanced argument provide the pressure around them.
passages.jane-eyre-1847-chapter-10-wide-world: After years shaped by Lowood’s rules, Jane imagines a world wider than the one she knows. Charlotte Brontë gives that desire a physical scale: a varied field stretches outward, carrying hopes and fears, sensations and perils together. Freedom is not presented as comfort. It asks for courage and a willingness to meet experience directly. The passage can hold many smaller journeys inside its forward movement, from confinement toward knowledge or from certainty toward risk. Attend to the words that widen the page for you. Your poem need not retell Jane’s departure; it can follow any honest route through the tension between safety, possibility and the unknown.
passages.middlemarch-1871-book-2-other-side-of-si: George Eliot pauses the story to consider how much ordinary human feeling goes unheard. Grass grows, a squirrel’s heart beats, and silence becomes a roar too large for a person to bear. The passage moves from tragedy to bodily protection with characteristic sharpness, ending on the uncomfortable shelter of stupidity. Its sounds and scales invite close reading: the nearly inaudible sits beside the overwhelming, while attention becomes both gift and danger. A poem found here might listen, resist, soften or turn away. Keep the words whose volume changes as you notice them, without needing to resolve Eliot’s difficult question about what human beings can bear to feel.
passages.douglass-1845-chapter-6-pathway-to-freed: Frederick Douglass recalls the moment he understood literacy as a pathway from enslavement toward freedom. Loss and discovery arrive together: an attempt to prevent his learning reveals why learning matters, and sadness is joined by hope and fixed purpose. The page carries the force of Douglass’s own historical argument, not an anonymous lesson about perseverance. Its words of instruction, difficulty, accident and resolve can be met without separating them from that authorship and context. Read for the movement from recognition into action. Any poem you find should remain your selection, while the source passage continues to name the conditions and the person from which its language comes.
passages.moby-dick-1851-chapter-1-watery-world: Ishmael introduces himself, then lets a dark turn of mind carry the sentence from an empty purse and damp streets toward the sea. Herman Melville’s famous opening is restless and physical: weather enters the soul, funeral processions cross the road, and water becomes a way to change one’s circulation. Humour, melancholy and escape move together rather than forming a single mood. The repetitions offer many places to step into or out of the current. Keep the words that shift your own weather. Your poem can stay ashore, set sail, or find another movement entirely, with Ishmael’s voice and Melville’s source still surrounding what remains.
passages.dorian-gray-1891-preface-art-and-beauty: Oscar Wilde’s preface gathers short declarations about artists, critics, beauty, morality, concealment and revelation. Each sentence sounds complete, yet neighbouring claims unsettle one another. That tension makes the page less a set of instructions than a bright field of positions to test. Words recur in altered relationships, inviting a maker to cross the boundaries of the aphorisms without pretending Wilde has said the resulting poem. Notice which terms attract or repel each other when their original sentences begin to fall away. You may find an argument, a contradiction, or something more private. The source remains visible so that your selection stays in conversation with Wilde’s deliberately provocative frame.
passages.alice-1865-chapter-1-daisy-chain: Alice sits beside her sister with nothing much to do, wavering between sleepiness and the small practical pleasure of making a daisy-chain. Then a White Rabbit passes, speaking and consulting a watch, and the ordinary afternoon tilts into strangeness. Lewis Carroll builds the change from familiar objects rather than announcing wonder in advance. The page offers boredom, pictures, conversation, heat, curiosity and sudden motion as possible openings. Follow whichever detail makes the scene move for you. Your poem need not chase the Rabbit or know the later adventure; it can remain by the bank, wake slowly, or discover another threshold in the words Carroll placed there.
passages.great-expectations-1861-chapter-9-memora: Pip looks back on one day and imagines a life as a long chain: iron or gold, thorns or flowers, formed link by link from a first remembered moment. Charles Dickens makes consequence tangible without deciding whether the chain is burden, treasure, wound or growth. The narrator asks the reader to pause, creating a small space between event and understanding. That balanced imagery gives a maker several directions through memory and change. Notice which material your words seem to take on as you select them. A poem may bind, flower, question or break away, while Pip’s retrospective voice and the source of the images remain clearly attached.
passages.yellow-wallpaper-1892-light-and-pattern: The confined narrator watches the wallpaper change as daylight gives way to moonlight. Pattern becomes bars; something hidden seems to move behind them; looking itself grows tense and uncertain. Charlotte Perkins Gilman’s repetition makes perception feel like both evidence and trap. The page should retain its context of coercive treatment and mental distress rather than becoming a decorative store of gothic images. Read for the shifts between light, paper, watching and movement, and choose without trying to diagnose or correct the narrator. Your poem can attend to enclosure, resistance, pattern or another pressure you notice, while Gilman’s authorship and the unsettling source remain in view.
passages.mrs-dalloway-1925-flowers-and-morning: Clarissa Dalloway steps into a June morning to buy flowers, and the present opens suddenly into remembered air, waves, windows and a feeling that something might happen. Virginia Woolf lets domestic intention, bodily sensation and time flow through one another before the party has begun. The page moves quickly in scale, from a London street to a childhood threshold and back into a mind alert to delight and foreboding. Listen for words that make the morning expand or catch. Your selection need not explain Clarissa or imitate the sentence’s movement; it can gather a quieter rhythm while Woolf’s source continues to hold the larger current.
passages.zitkala-sa-1921-impressions-wild-freedom: Zitkala-Sa remembers herself at seven, moving freely with the wind and taking courage from her mother’s teaching. Hair, fire, fear, spirit and motion make the recollection immediate, but the page is not anonymous material about childhood or an interchangeable account of Indigenous life. It belongs to a Dakota writer naming her own experience and relationship. Keep that authorship present as you read for the physical energy of the sentences and the forms of freedom they hold. A poem might follow movement, kinship, bravery or the elements, but it should arise from your attention rather than flattening the cultural and personal context surrounding the words.
passages.my-antonia-1918-prairie-transfiguration: Jim Burden remembers the Nebraska prairie in autumn, where red grass, fierce sunlight and moving shadows make the land feel transformed. Willa Cather brings material detail and mythic scale close together: fields become gold, fire suggests both victory and death, and ordinary change takes on the force of transfiguration. The language can support wonder without requiring a single pastoral mood. Look for colours, movements and temperatures that alter one another when only a few words remain. Your poem may stay close to the earth or follow the scene into memory and legend, while the novel’s remembered landscape continues to surround the new path you choose.
passages.dubliners-1914-eveline-evening: Eveline sits at a window while evening gathers in the avenue. Dust, footsteps, a field, bright roofs and a familiar organ tune draw past and present into the room before her planned departure. James Joyce builds pressure from ordinary sensory details rather than announcing the choice outright. Home can feel sheltering, exhausted, vanished or difficult to leave, sometimes within the same phrase. Attend to what approaches and what recedes across the page. A poem found here might remain still, cross a threshold, or listen to memory without deciding for Eveline. Her specific story and Joyce’s source remain visible around the words you keep.
passages.north-and-south-1855-milton-smoke: Margaret Hale approaches the industrial town of Milton through air changed by smoke. Elizabeth Gaskell layers cloud, frost, lost fragrance, streets and a strange factory comparison until arrival becomes something seen, smelled and felt. The description carries social meaning without turning the town into a simple emblem; unfamiliarity shapes Margaret’s first impression. Read for the materials that thicken or clear the scene, and for motion inside what initially looks fixed. Your poem can follow colour, labour, displacement or another thread in the language. Keep the words that form a truthful route for you while Gaskell’s setting and perspective stay attached to their source.
passages.time-machine-1895-flowing-years: The Time Traveller describes accelerating beyond the ordinary pace of days and nights. The sun hops, darkness arrives like a wing, buildings rise with impossible speed, and a snail seems to race across the ground. H. G. Wells turns duration into visible movement, making familiar measures of time strange enough to handle. Verbs and reversals give the passage a playful energy even as the traveller loses his usual place in the world. Choose the words that change speed when set beside one another. Your poem may rush, pause, build or dissolve, without needing to explain the machine or continue the journey beyond this page.
passages.jekyll-hyde-1886-truly-two: Near the end of his account, Henry Jekyll tries to describe a self he has discovered to be divided. Robert Louis Stevenson gives that division spatial and bodily force through truth, shipwreck, intelligence and a crowd of inner denizens. The passage belongs to a character explaining dangerous choices, not to a clinical statement about identity. Its language nevertheless opens many paths through doubleness, concealment, knowledge and responsibility. Read for the point where certainty begins to split. Your poem can accept, resist or rearrange those terms, while the source remains present to distinguish your selection from Jekyll’s confession and Stevenson’s larger design.
passages.age-of-innocence-1920-loneliness-and-pre: Newland Archer and Ellen Olenska speak inside the closely watched social world of old New York. Edith Wharton lets gesture and withheld feeling carry as much weight as direct speech: hands, kindness, unpleasant truth, loneliness and tears press against the demand to maintain appearances. The scene’s restraint creates several possible emotional routes without offering easy innocence. Notice what the characters can name and what remains protected by manners or silence. A poem found here might expose, shelter, refuse or ask, but it need not settle their relationship. Keep the words that alter the balance for you while Wharton’s social setting remains around them.
passages.awakening-1899-voice-of-the-sea: The narrator pauses over Edna Pontellier’s emerging awareness and turns toward the sea. Kate Chopin’s language moves among beginnings, worlds, tangles, voices, wandering, touch and embrace, making consciousness feel both solitary and bodily. The page does not reduce awakening to a simple liberation; uncertainty and depth travel with it. Read for the words that call from a distance and those that seem close to the skin. Your poem might enter the water, remain at its edge, or follow an entirely different voice through the passage. Edna’s context and Chopin’s source stay visible so that the selection does not pretend to replace them.
passages.pointed-firs-1896-dunnet-landing: A narrator returns to Dunnet Landing and sees the coastal village as both place and remembered relationship. Sarah Orne Jewett gathers rocky shore, dark woods, tree-nailed houses, knowing windows, flowers, harbour and firs into a landscape shaped by long acquaintance. Affection lives in physical details rather than in a declaration that the village is perfect. The page offers shelter, distance, endurance and welcome without forcing them into one mood. Choose the words that make a place appear for you, whether familiar or newly seen. Your poem can arrive, remember or look outward while Jewett’s village and the source of its language remain clearly present.

journeys.thresholds-and-departures: This five-page path begins beside Alice’s riverbank, where an ordinary afternoon tips into pursuit. Jane Eyre then imagines leaving the rules of Lowood for a wider field of experience, while Margaret Hale approaches an industrial city whose air already announces change. Eveline pauses at a window before a departure she has planned, and the Time Traveller finally crosses beyond ordinary movement altogether. The sequence does not insist that leaving is brave, necessary or complete. It offers thresholds with different pressures and consequences. Keep one poem from each page and notice how curiosity, fear, memory, arrival and velocity alter the meaning of the next step.
journeys.light-and-hidden-worlds: This five-page path follows changing light through different kinds of attention. Clarissa Dalloway enters a June morning alive with memory; Jim Burden sees prairie grass and sun turn the land almost mythic; a remembered coastal village appears through windows, flowers and firs. The light then narrows inside the room of The Yellow Wallpaper, where looking becomes confinement and resistance, before Middlemarch asks how much ordinary life human perception can bear. The sequence moves from brightness toward difficult forms of seeing without treating light as simple hope. Keep one poem from each page and let every new field revise what visibility, concealment and attention can mean.
journeys.divided-and-becoming: This five-page path begins with Anne Elliot reconsidering the prudence that shaped her youth. Frederick Douglass then recognises literacy as a route toward freedom and fixes his purpose to learn. Victor Frankenstein imagines breaking the bounds of life and death; Edna Pontellier’s consciousness stirs toward the sea; Henry Jekyll names a division he can no longer contain. Knowledge changes each speaker, but the sequence does not claim that every change is liberating or wise. Keep one poem from each page, carrying questions of counsel, learning, ambition, awakening and responsibility forward. The path leaves room for becoming to include refusal, consequence and contradiction.
